item.title: Understanding the Nonfarm Payroll Data
item.description:
Nonfarm payrolls

I. What the number is

  • Definition: The nonfarm payroll data measure 80% of paid workers who contribute to GDP in the U.S.1
  • Source & Frequency: The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) collects payroll data from private and government entities on a monthly basis and usually publishes the data on the first Friday of each month at 8:30 a.m. ET.
  • Reference Period: The CES defines employment as persons on the establishment payrolls who work or receive payments for any part of the pay period that includes the 12th day of the month.2
  • The Measure Excludes: farm employees, active-duty military members, unpaid volunteers for non-profit organizations, sole proprietors, and private household employees.3

Why are certain groups excluded?

  • Agriculture
    • CES draws its sample based on administrative records from the Office of Unemployment Insurance (UI). This means workers who are not covered under the government’s unemployment insurance program wouldn’t be counted. In agriculture, however, workers tend to have exemptions to requirements for unemployment coverage.
    • In addition, businesses are frequently family-owned (i.e. sole proprietors), which make them out of scope for CES.4
    • Lastly, the sample size for farming would be too small to make statistically sound estimates (0.9%–1.2% of total employment).5
    • This doesn’t mean that farming employment is completely unaccounted for. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) conducts surveys twice every year to collect data on agricultural workers.
  • Military: The nonfarm payroll report primarily covers employment that is associated with the business cycle. Military employment changes primarily based on the need for national defense, not the performance of the economy.

II. How the number is made

The sample and the census

The birth-death model

[WRITE. The thing to establish first is that this is two mechanisms, not one, and almost every popular criticism is aimed at the smaller of the two.]

  1. Imputation. BLS “excludes employment losses due to business deaths from sample-based estimation in order to offset the missing employment gains from business births” — in practice, “not reflecting sample units going out of business and imputing to them the same trend as the other firms in the sample.”10 BLS says this step “accounts for most of the birth and death employment.”
  2. An ARIMA model on the residual only, estimating “the residual birth-death employment not accounted for by the imputation,” fitted on the trailing five years.11

[SIZE — so the reader can judge for themselves. Net birth-death, total nonfarm, as forecast: +372,000 across April–December 2025 (nine months) and +861,000 across January–August 2026 (eight months).12 Set that against the −911,000 benchmark and let the reader do the arithmetic rather than doing it for them.]

[WRITE — the mechanism of failure, which is not the one people name. The model does not “invent” jobs; it assumes deaths are a usable proxy for unobserved births. Michael Horrigan — 33 years at BLS, six of them running employment measurement — puts the failure mode in one sentence: “If employment losses from firm deaths begin exceeding employment gains from new firms, using deaths as a proxy for unobserved births will result in an overestimation of job creation.”13 That is a statement about the economy, not about the statistics.]

[THE COMPARISON THAT DOES THE WORK — the 2009 benchmark revision was −902,000; the 2025 preliminary was −911,000.14 Sixteen years apart, effectively the same number, both in or near a downturn. Decide what you think that similarity means before you write Part IV.]

[FIXES ALREADY MADE — quarterly updates since the January 2011 benchmark cut the forecast horizon from up to 21 months to at most 12.15 Effective with preliminary January 2026 estimates, BLS modified the ARIMA component “by incorporating current sample information to inform the forecasts,” applied retroactively to April–December 2025.16]

A Falling Response Rate

[WRITE — the point is the gap between column one and column three. The share of units answering has fallen roughly 18 points since 2016. The share of employment collected by final closing has barely moved. Both are true because collection is employment-weighted: the large employers still report. What the survey is losing is small establishments — which is the same population the birth-death model is extrapolating over.

Resist the temptation to assert that this causes the revisions. State the overlap and say what evidence would settle it.]

Seasonal adjustment

Seasonal adjustments make it easier to determine whether an employment change is due to normal changes throughout the year or an indicator of anomalies.

  • The question seasonal adjustment answers is “what does a normal January look like?” X-11, the engine inside X-13, answers it by averaging, not by fitting a model. Take the same calendar month across several years and average it — that is your estimate of what that month normally does. Divide it out of the raw series and what is left is trend plus noise. Smooth that to get a cleaner trend, take the trend back out, re-estimate the monthly pattern on the cleaner residual, and go round again. After three or four passes the estimate stops moving. [The particular moving averages have names — 2×12, 3×3, 3×5, Henderson — but the names are not the idea. One parenthetical at most.]
  • Two things follow directly from averaging rather than fitting, and they are the reason Part III exists at all. First, every new observation changes the average, so last January’s factor moves when this January arrives. Second, the newest months sit at the end of the sample with no future to average over — so X-13 forecasts the series forward and averages over the forecast. Those are the least stable factors in the series.
  • CES runs this concurrently: factors are recomputed every month with the latest data rather than fixed in advance, and the models are re-specified annually.17 X-13 wraps X-11 in a regARIMA step that first strips out outliers, trading-day effects and moving holidays (CES adjusts for Easter and Labor Day) so the averaging is not contaminated by them.
  • The seasonally adjusted history changes every month even when not one additional survey response arrives

[WRITE — the scale of the adjustment. Month-over-month change in total nonfarm payrolls each January, thousands, as first published:]

[The point: the headline is a residual. Roughly three million jobs genuinely come off payrolls every January; the adjustment adds back very slightly less; the difference is what gets reported and argued about. A 5% error in an adjustment that size would be 150,000 — larger than most of the monthly prints in this table.]

III. How the number changes

Three structurally different operations all get called “a revision,” and they have different causes, sizes and meanings.

Two traps worth naming for the reader: the “final sample-based estimate” is not final — the benchmark is still coming; and the number in the news is usually the preliminary benchmark, which itself gets revised.

The monthly cycle

CES “revises its initial monthly estimates twice, in the immediately succeeding 2 months, to incorporate additional sample receipts from respondents in the survey.”18

[WRITE — July 2026 is the example: the initial print said the economy lost 23,000 jobs; one month of additional survey responses flipped it to a gain of 21,000. Same month, same method, opposite sign.]

The annual benchmark

The final benchmark is published with the January preliminary estimates in early February, and affects 21 months of previously published data, anchored to March of the previous year.19

[WRITE — the split almost nobody mentions: the 12 months up to the March anchor get the QCEW treatment; the 9 months after it are only rescaled and re-modelled. BofA states the consequence plainly: April–December 2025 payrolls “will not be revised based on the QCEW until 2027.”20 So a payroll number is roughly eighteen months old before anyone checks it against tax records.]

Also worth folding in: five years of seasonally adjusted data are recalculated with every benchmark.21 Months far outside the 21-month window change every February from seasonal factors alone.

Decomposition of Revisions

The decomposition is arithmetic on two vintages of the same month:

The unadjusted series never touches a seasonal factor, so anything that moves it is incoming data. Whatever is left when you subtract that from the adjusted revision is the adjustment changing its mind. [Say plainly that the cross-term — revised data being re-adjusted by revised factors — falls into the second bucket, so read it as “factors, and everything that interacts with them.”]

[WRITE — the finding. Total nonfarm, September 2022 to July 2026, 47 months:]

  • The drift is data. Mean total revision −61k; mean data component −50k, mean factor component −11k. Payrolls have been revised down persistently, and late reporting plus the benchmark explains most of it.
  • The noise is not. Mean absolute factor component is 48k against 71k for data, and the factor component is the larger of the two in 20 of 47 months.
  • The two pull in opposite directions in 26 of 47 months (correlation −0.46). The published revision routinely understates how much actually moved underneath it.
  • October 2024 is the month to lead with: the revision as published was +21k. Underneath, late responses took −84k off and seasonal re-estimation put +105k back. Nothing about that month was quiet.
  • January 2025 runs the other way: −191k total, of which only −55k was data. −136k came from re-estimated seasonal factors — in the month where, per Table 3, the adjustment is already doing roughly three million jobs of work.

[CAVEAT TO STATE, NOT BURY — the data component mixes two of the three mechanisms in the vocabulary table: late survey responses and the benchmark. Months inside a benchmark window carry both. Don’t let the reader assume it is all late responses.]

[CHECK BEFORE PUBLISHING — October 2025 onward. The October 2025 employment report was cancelled during the shutdown, which shifts the vintage-counting logic in fetch_nfp_vintages.py by one release slot. Verify Oct–Dec 2025 against the published vintages before quoting those months.]

[OPTIONAL SECOND CUT — your report also splits the same total by stage (first revision / second revision / everything after). That one maps straight onto the vocabulary table and would make a clean companion panel if the post has room.]

IV. What happened in 2024–2026

Benchmark (to March) Preliminary Final
March 2024 −818,000 −598,000
March 2025 −911,000 −862,000
March 2026 −79,000 pending Feb 2027

[WRITE — the arc. A −911k revision fed a year of “the data is fake” arguments. BLS changed the birth-death model effective January 2026. The next preliminary benchmark came in at −79,000 and was released on 28 August 2026 to near-silence.]

[WHY THIS SITS HERE — Part IV turns on whether the labour market actually weakened, and this is evidence for that independent of any benchmark revision. Read it left to right.

Two cautions before you lean on it: the reference distribution runs to 2025, so it contains the 2021–22 hiring boom, which makes “normal” look strong; and a z-score says unusual for that industry, not large. Say what the panel shows and let the reader weigh it.]

[THE OPEN QUESTION YOU CAN TAKE A POSITION ON — is that the model fix working, or just a calmer labour market? Note the Cleveland Fed finds 1980–2025 benchmark revisions have a mean of −4.51k and a median of −2.00k, and that structural-break tests find no break — so 2024–25 was extreme but not a regime change.22]

Questions worth further exploration

Is the CES sample shrinking, and does it matter? The August 2026 technical note puts the sample at 119,000 businesses and 622,000 worksites, against 121,000 and 631,000 a year earlier — a decline of roughly 1.5%. Over the same period the stated coverage moved from “about one-third” of nonfarm payroll jobs to “approximately 26 percent.” A 1.5% reduction in the sample cannot produce a shift of that size, so either the denominator changed or BLS restated the basis. This is a separate question from Table 2 — that one is about who answers, this one is about how many are asked. [Worth running down — if the sample really is contracting, the standard error on every monthly print is widening, and nobody is writing about it.]

Can the adjustment be reproduced? X-13ARIMA-SEATS is public — the Census Bureau distributes the binary and the seasonal package wraps it in R. Feed it the unadjusted payroll series, compare your factors against the published ones, and you have a direct test of how much of any given revision the adjustment can account for. [Worth doing: it turns Part II from something you read into something you checked. The interesting version is running it on two vintages of the same series and watching the factors move.]

Corrections made to the previous draft

  1. \bullet replaced with markdown -. LaTeX macros don’t render in HTML.
  2. Sample size was 121,000 / 631,000 — the current figure is 119,000 / 622,000, ~26% of nonfarm jobs, per the August 2026 technical note. The old numbers are a prior vintage.
  3. The QCEW 97% figure was cited to benchmark-tables.htm, which is an index page and doesn’t contain it. The real source is the CES National Benchmark Article, and the precise claim is 97% of nonfarm employment within the scope of the establishment survey — not 97% of all US employment.
  4. The seasonal-adjustment example used farming, which nonfarm payrolls exclude. Needs replacing.
  5. The revision schedule was listed three times in three forms. Replaced with one vocabulary table plus Figure 1.

Still open

  • QCEW establishment count — settled at 12.1 million (2025), with a quotable sentence from the Employment and Wages annual averages publication. Your 12,238,200 from the BLS video is the same order and is probably a different vintage or a quarterly count, but cite the publication rather than the video — a YouTube link is a weak reference for a post graded on sourcing.
  • Publication lag: your draft said five months and BofA says five, but BLS’s own wording is “within 6 months after the end of each referenced quarter.” Use BLS’s, or say “about five to six months.”
  • Still missing from this folder — fig-release-schedule.png, fig-benchmark-window.png, fig-successive-windows.png. The post already links all three, so the render will show broken images until they are exported from the design canvas. figure1.png and fig-revision-decomposition.png are in place.
